title: National Equipment Rental, Ltd. v. Szukhent (1964)
summary: A stranger named in a printed lease to receive process for the lessees was an “agent authorized by appointment” under the Federal Rules once she promptly accepted the papers and mailed them to the lessees; the Court expressly left open the case in which the appointed agent gives no prompt notice.
notes:
This makes a useful Contracts connection concerning standardized agreements and procedural consent, but the governing service question and the broader fairness of the bargain remain distinct.

The Szukhents, a father and son farming in Michigan, leased two incubators from the New York company on a printed form; the decision was 6-3 with Justice Stewart writing, Justice Black dissenting alone, and Justice Brennan dissenting joined by Chief Justice Warren and Justice Goldberg.

sections.Parties: National Equipment Rental, Ltd., a corporation with its principal place of business in New York, leased farm equipment to the respondents and was the plaintiff below and petitioner. The Szukhents, a father and son farming in Michigan, were the lessees, defendants and respondents. Florence Weinberg, the person the lease designated to receive process for them in New York, was not a party. The lessor wanted to sue in New York for unpaid rent; the Szukhents sought to quash service on the ground that Weinberg was not their agent.
sections.Material Facts: In 1961 the Szukhents leased farm equipment on a printed form less than a page and a half long, with eighteen numbered paragraphs. The last paragraph, printed just above their signatures in the same type as the rest, deemed the agreement made in Nassau County, New York, chose New York law, and designated Florence Weinberg, of 47-21 Forty-first Street, Long Island City, as agent for the purpose of accepting service of any process within New York. The Szukhents did not know her; the company had chosen her, and it emerged after suit that she was the wife of one of its officers. In 1962 the company sued in federal court in New York alleging missed rental payments. A marshal delivered two copies of the summons and complaint to Weinberg, who mailed them to the Szukhents the same day with a letter saying she had been served as their agent.
sections.Procedural History: The District Court for the Eastern District of New York quashed service: although Weinberg had promptly notified the Szukhents and sent the papers, the lease did not explicitly require her to do so, so there was a failure of the agency arrangement to achieve intrinsic and continuing reality. The Second Circuit affirmed, 311 F.2d 79. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and reversed and remanded on January 6, 1964. Justice Stewart wrote for a five-Justice majority; Justice Black dissented alone, and Justice Brennan, joined by Chief Justice Warren and Justice Goldberg, dissented separately. The question arose under Rule 4(d)(1), now Rule 4(e)(2)(C).
sections.Issue: Was a person designated in a printed lease to receive process for the lessees, who was a stranger to them and whose appointment did not expressly require her to forward process, an agent authorized by appointment to receive service under the Federal Rules, where she in fact promptly transmitted the summons and complaint to them?
sections.Holding: Yes. Parties to a contract may agree in advance to submit to a court’s jurisdiction, to permit notice to be served by the opposing party, or even to waive notice altogether. Under general agency principles, Weinberg’s prompt acceptance and transmittal of the papers validated the agency without an express promise to forward them, so service on her was valid. The Rule sets a uniform federal standard, and neither Michigan nor New York law required an express undertaking to notify the principal. The holding was confined to the case in which prompt notice was actually given; the Court did not reach a case in which the defendant received no personal notice.
sections.Reasoning: The Court first set aside Wuchter v. Pizzutti, which concerned the Fourteenth Amendment limits on a state statute designating a public official to receive process for nonresidents; the question here was whether a private contract could appoint an agent within the meaning of a Federal Rule. The clause’s purpose was plain: the company inserted it, and the Szukhents agreed, so that litigation under the lease would take place in New York, and it was settled that contracting parties may agree in advance to jurisdiction, to service by the adversary, or to waive notice altogether. Applying general agency law, Weinberg’s prompt acceptance and transmittal of the papers under the authority the lease conferred was itself sufficient to validate the agency even without an advance promise to forward process. The alleged conflict of interest ignored the narrow agency: Weinberg was appointed for the single purpose of receiving service, both sides shared an interest in timely notice, and nothing suggested she had a pecuniary stake. Had she not promptly notified the Szukhents, a claim might well be made that her failure invalidated the agency.

learning.why: Service on the contractually named New York agent was effective where she accepted the task and promptly notified the Michigan defendants.

topics.cp-service: The named contractual agent’s acceptance and prompt notification supported effective service in the case before the Court.
topics.cp-notice: Actual prompt transmission of the process was central to the narrow holding.
topics.cp-consent-jurisdiction: The contract appointed an agent for service, raising an issue different from whether minimum contacts independently existed.
topics.forum-selection: The case illustrates contractual arrangements affecting the litigation forum without collapsing every such arrangement into a forum clause.
topics.cp-frcp-4: The question was whether the contractual designee was an 'agent authorized by appointment' to receive process under Rule 4.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Black dissented: the Szukhents had never heard of Weinberg, the company handpicked her, and only after suit did it emerge that she was an officer’s wife; the appointment was invalid under New York law, and calling their signature knowing consent to suit in New York was “a fiction—not even an amiable one.” He predicted such clauses would spread through the boilerplate of equipment leases and conditional sales contracts. Justice Brennan, joined by Chief Justice Warren and Justice Goldberg, would have required no conflicting interest, an explicit condition that the agent transmit process forthwith, and proof beyond a signature that an individual understandingly consented to be sued away from home.

mnemonic.rationale: Incubators and an agent for service
